before.name: Caselle
before.description: Connect fund accounting, utility billing, and payments for small and mid-size cities - exhibited at GFOA 2026

paragraphs: Caselle makes government accounting, ERP, and payments software. It is right-sized, in the company's words, for small to medium local governments, cities, and districts.

Accounting, utility billing, and reporting run in one system whose modules pass data to each other. Built-in tools produce audit-ready statements and track budgets in real time. Payroll and human resources are covered as well. So are permits and code enforcement. Business licensing and tax collection sit in the same system. A further set of tools is meant for sharing information with residents and collecting feedback.

Caselle dates its commitment to community to 1978. The company says its story began with Duane Hutchings, a CPA in Spanish Fork, Utah. Working with his sons and Spanish Fork City, he developed software to improve the workflows of people in local government. In 2024 Caselle joined Govineer Solutions. A published case study describes a city choosing Caselle after an extensive RFP process. That study says McPherson, Kansas explored six different government accounting software solutions before choosing Caselle. It reports the city saved four full workdays each month after the transition.

paragraphs: Aurigo Software sells capital program management software to government agencies that plan, build and maintain public infrastructure. It also serves facility owners in areas such as data centers, life sciences, manufacturing, and energy and utilities. The company's platform, Masterworks, brings planning, execution, financials, right of way and analytics together in one system.

On the delivery side it coordinates contracts, schedules, costs and field work so teams can hold to the original plan and keep a complete audit trail. Compliance, funding transparency and governance are meant to sit inside everyday work so public money stays accountable. Agencies can change forms, workflows, business rules and dashboards through configuration rather than code. An AI layer called Lumina supports decision-making with compliance and governance built in, and the company says every insight and recommendation it produces can be audited and traced.

Cities, counties, transit agencies and transportation departments across North America use the platform to manage capital programs, replace legacy systems and automate federal reimbursements. The company claims more than 300 customers and over 20 years of capital program expertise behind the product. It also says the software monitors project signals to catch cost, schedule and delivery risks before they turn critical.

before.name: B2Gnow
before.description: Supplier diversity and DBE compliance tracking SaaS for states, cities, airports, and transit

paragraphs: B2Gnow sells compliance software to public agencies and the contractors on their projects, covering vendor programs, prevailing wage labor compliance and grant management. The company lists states, state DOTs, cities, counties, transit agencies, airports, education, general contractors and healthcare among the kinds of clients it names.

The vendor side is a cloud-based platform covering DBE, MBE, WBE and SBE compliance initiatives. Certification work runs from online applications through agency review to approval. For contract compliance, prime and subcontractor payments are collected, and subcontractors confirm payment directly, monthly or quarterly. Reporting draws on more than 400 standard system reports. A payroll line covers Davis-Bacon and Related Acts, the Service Contract Act, state prevailing wage laws and local living wage ordinances. Grant work runs through BlackCat, from applications to asset management and spend-down tracking.

The company says the software has been implemented at over 400 organizations. It claims one million users regularly access the system to register, prequalify, submit reports, manage grants and review bid solicitations. The site cites over 25 years of vendor program compliance experience. B2Gnow and eComply have joined together into one platform spanning vendor management and labor compliance. Hosting is described as fully redundant, with guaranteed availability of 99.9% and SOC 2 Type 2 certification.

before.name: bids&tenders
before.description: eProcurement bid management and supplier portal for Canadian and US agencies (Valsoft, 2025)

paragraphs: bids&tenders sells a digital procurement platform that centralizes procurement activities and streamlines the processes around them. Buyers create and post bids to a branded self-service portal, or send invitations to prequalified suppliers, configuring projects from a template or a custom setup. Registered suppliers, supplier questions and electronic submissions are managed in one central platform, where a compliance checker screens bids before evaluation.

Evaluation templates and online evaluations feed automatic bid analysis and a digital scorecard. Contract management covers contracts, expiry notifications, purchase orders, change orders and insurance certificates online. Reporting tracks spend, team resource loading and upcoming project tasks. Add-on modules offered to agencies include Award Approvals, Contract Builder with DocuSign, Supplier Performance, Open Data and Single Sign-On.

The Kinetic GPO announcement describes an eProcurement platform for public sector organizations across Canada and the United States. The same page states the platform is used by government agencies, municipalities, utilities, healthcare organizations, educational institutions, and engineering and construction firms across Canada and the United States. Since November 2025, bids&tenders has been part of Valsoft Corporation.

A vendor dashboard saves keyword searches and agency watchlists. Vendors can search open RFPs, ITBs and other contracting opportunities. Those searches can specify keyword tags and commodity codes. On the agency side, setting up a new solicitation for vendor bid submission takes moments. Submitted bids are then reviewed through a bid review dashboard.

Agencies from coast to coast use it to publish contracting opportunities. The agencies browsable by region include the Kentucky Community and Technical College System. Seattle Public Schools also appears on that list.

before.description: Playground safety inspections plus Park Protector inspection/asset software for munis and schools

paragraphs: Playground Guardian sells onsite safety inspection of playground equipment and surfacing, checking that they meet safety standards. The company also sells Park Protector, a playground inspection and asset management application that runs on a computer or mobile device. Playground Guardian is based in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Park Protector records inspections on any device with or without cell service, and is built to CPSC Publication 325 and ASTM standards. The surface testing module captures the data fields required by ASTM F1292 and F3313, including HIC, Gmax, impact velocity, and drop height. Inspections, surface tests, issues, work orders, and complaints export to PDF or Excel.

Park Protector is offered for managing inspections across city-owned play spaces and facilities. The software page names parks, school districts, and municipal facilities across the United States. Park Protector is presented for organizations ranging from solo CPSI inspectors to large municipal departments. Organizations that already have maintenance staff managing their facilities are offered the Park Protector app.

quote.text: Park Protector replaces clipboards, spreadsheets, and disconnected tools with a single app built around how inspection professionals actually work: in the field, across dozens of locations, with or without a signal.

before.name: Athletify
before.description: Staff scheduling software built for parks and rec departments (flat annual pricing)

paragraphs: Athletify makes staff scheduling software for parks and recreation departments, pulling every program and every worker into one schedule that a manager can filter as needed. Staff need only one login even when they hold several positions.

Shifts can be filtered and grouped by program, location, position, or staff member, and the views a department reaches for most often can be saved. Requests to drop a shift, claim a shift, or take time off arrive in a centralized inbox that all admins share. Age limitation tools let a department create and enforce scheduling rules for younger workers, including restrictions that keep them off early morning or late evening shifts. Messaging is built in, with channels for different staff groups such as lifeguards or referees.

The company says it has heard from hundreds of cities about the struggle of managing staff, and it is looking for beta partners to help shape the tool. Pricing is advertised without tiers or per-user fees. The site dates the beta program as running until July 1, 2025.

before.name: MyVolunteer
before.description: Volunteer registration and tracking with integrated background screening (CRC product)

paragraphs: MyVolunteer is a volunteer management platform covering recruitment, scheduling, tracking, and reporting. Onboarding runs on customizable forms and automated processes, and the platform tracks volunteer hours and generates reports on impact and performance. Volunteers themselves get a self-service portal for managing their schedules, hours, and profiles.

In healthcare the platform is aimed at hospitals, clinics, and healthcare organizations, and handles background checks, ongoing criminal monitoring, and certification tracking. The K-12 school version manages parent volunteers, classroom aides, and event helpers, and checks that individuals meet background check requirements. Government agencies are named as a third market, with screening and volunteer tracking set against federal, state, and local regulations.

The product was developed by background screening experts and integrates with a background and criminal monitoring platform. The about page names nonprofits, schools, healthcare providers, and government agencies as the organizations the company works with.

paragraphs: NEOGOV sells human resources software for government agencies, built around public sector hiring, onboarding, and compliance. The platform is described as purpose-built for government agencies, municipalities, and the broader public sector, with forms, workflows, and reporting aligned to public sector regulations. Products named on the site include Insight for applicant tracking, Attract for candidate relationship management, and Onboard for employee onboarding.

Insight is presented as an applicant tracking system that automates and centralizes recruitment activities for public sector hiring. Insight supports civil service requirements such as minimum qualifications screening, canvassing letters, and ranked eligibility lists, according to that page. Attract is a candidate relationship management system for agencies to engage candidates who have expressed interest in government jobs.

GovernmentJobs.com is offered as a job board built for public sector recruitment, with jobs posted in Insight published there automatically. The site also lists onboarding, performance management, learning management, custom forms, background investigations, and compliance management among the functions covered.

paragraphs: CIMS sells cemetery management software that keeps maps, records and finances in one place. It is used by municipal, faith-based, private, and association-managed cemeteries of all sizes across the United States and Canada.

The top tier connects interment and ownership records to GIS smart maps of the cemetery grounds. The platform is cloud-based, reachable from anywhere with an internet connection. Packages are tiered, and every tier includes core cemetery management tools. Ground penetrating radar data can be brought into any of the three tiers. Drone imagery supplies high-resolution photos for the maps. An add-on called Burial Search lets the public look up records on the web, a smartphone, or an on-site kiosk.

For cemeteries still on paper, the company moves analog or digital records into the new database. It states that more than 1,200 cemeteries have invested in CIMS. A page for Catholic customers says it helps dioceses and parishes protect burial records. Subscriptions include unlimited training and technical support at no additional charge.

paragraphs: EPIC iO sells AI-driven monitoring for physical sites, along with the wireless connectivity that keeps those locations online. Its named settings are utilities, oil and gas, construction, retail and industrial sites. Both sides run on a software platform the company calls EPIC Cortex.

The video analysis is meant to separate security events from environmental activity such as weather or wildlife, which cuts false alarms. License plate recognition adds vehicle awareness at site entrances, along the perimeter and for vehicle activity on site. For police use, the LPR page says the system alerts officers and dispatchers within seconds. On the connectivity side, the company offers primary, backup and failover links across 5G, satellite and fixed networks. The same platform centralizes SIM and device management across multiple carriers with real-time usage monitoring.

For public safety and critical infrastructure customers, EPIC iO frames its role as situational awareness that supports emergency response without replacing established response protocols. Homepage testimonials are attributed anonymously, by role, to bodies such as a municipal public safety agency. The about page names an AI platform called DeepInsights as the cornerstone of its mission.

before.name: Amilia
before.description: SmartRec activity registration and facility management platform

paragraphs: Amilia sells software that pulls memberships, program registration, payments, and reporting into one system. The customer it describes is the community organization that runs classes, memberships, and facilities for local families.

Registration happens through a branded online store that can stand on its own or sit inside the organization's existing website. Age or skill restrictions and defined registration periods control who can sign up for which activity. Waitlists fill open spots as soon as a registration is cancelled. On the facilities side, a calendar keeps bookings, activities, and rental contracts in sync so staff can see which space is in use and when. Access rules decide which memberships, activities, or passes open the door at each entry point.
The company states that over 1,500 organizations have chosen it. It advertises a 99.99% uptime guarantee for round-the-clock selling. Help is offered by live chat, phone, and email.

before.name: TeamLinkt
before.description: Free team and league management platform monetized via payments and ads; $8.3M Series A 2025

paragraphs: TeamLinkt sells sports registration, scheduling, and administration software to the organizations that run seasons. Registration forms are built inside the platform and payments are collected online, and schedules are published from the same place. An app puts schedules, scores, standings, and updates in front of athletes and their families, with team chat in place of scattered texts and email chains.

League operators get tools for building balanced schedules, tracking standings, assigning officials, and running game day operations across divisions. Clubs and associations get registration templates, rostering, scheduling across fields, courts, and ice times, and tracking of waivers, background checks, and certifications. Governing bodies register and manage their member clubs and associations, track compliance across them, and can run their own competitions.

Core features are free, with a paid bundle for organizations that want more advanced tools. An account is offered with no contract and no credit card. Support is offered over live chat rather than a ticket based queue.

quote.text: TeamLinkt brings every piece of your season into one platform, helping you deliver fair, on-time games with less manual work and fewer tools to juggle.

before.name: PlotBox
before.description: Cloud cemetery and crematory management with georectified GIS mapping for munis and funeral groups

paragraphs: PlotBox sells software for running cemeteries, crematories and funeral homes. The company pitches it as a way to centralise the key functions of a deathcare operation in one easy-to-use platform.

Mapping tools let staff visualise a cemetery layout, manage plot inventory and track burial locations. Scheduling covers cremations, burials and services across multiple locations. Finance modules handle invoicing, payments, receipts and trust fund management. A public-facing side gives families a search tool for finding the resting places of relatives.

Sean and Leona McAllister founded the company, which combines deathcare management software with georectified mapping. It reports over 130 employees globally. Case studies describe work with Calderdale Council on its bereavement services operations. Another covers Liverpool City Council and its cremation services.

before.scope_note: Homepage states it serves "cities, counties, townships, special districts, school districts, utilities, and state agencies across the United States," claims 2,000+ governments and 4,500+ implementations, and names Tucson, Orlando, Minneapolis, San Antonio, Miami, Tampa, Kansas City, San Diego, Boston, LA, Taylor County and others. Every named buyer is public. Note for the board: the site is much broader than our "Permitting & Licensing" category - it leads with finance/budgeting, procurement, public works and utilities alongside community development.
before.sled_only_why: Gov IT & Cyber run 2026-09-11: buyer stated as General government, led by finance (ERP, budgeting, procurement); also public works (asset management), community development (permitting), utilities (utility billing), and some school districts and t
before.acquisition_note: Acquired: Cartegraph (operations/asset management; announced 2022, Cox-financed), iGovServices ('Tax & Revenue', May 1, 2024), Ignatius (low-code forms/workflow, Feb 11, 2025). Itself: Cox Enterprises acquired majority ownership, Feb 27, 2024, at a $1.8B valuation.

paragraphs: OpenGov sells a cloud platform for cities, counties, and state agencies that connects budgeting, finance, permitting, and asset management in one system. The Public Service Platform brings ERP and Community Operations products together, spanning Financial Management, Budgeting & Performance, Procurement & Contract Management, Permitting & Licensing, 311 Request Management, Utility Billing, and Payroll. OG Assist is the AI assistant built into every product, helping staff find answers, draft documents, and complete guided actions across the platform.

Software is built specifically for cities, counties, and state agencies, and the pages say over 2,000 governments run day-to-day operations on it. The buyers named are cities, counties, townships, special districts, school districts, utilities, and state agencies across the United States. Compliance controls built in cover GASB, FEMA, HUD, ARPA, and FLSA, and the platform is stated to be SOC 2 compliant.

OpenGov states 4,500+ government software implementations completed, with timelines that vary by product and organizational complexity, typically ranging from 3 to 6 months. Government App Builder is a no-code platform that lets IT teams build custom forms, workflows, and citizen-facing apps, with permissions, audit logs, and version history.

acquired.deal: Acquired by Banyan Software on 12 June 2024, terms undisclosed; founder Bob Cote stayed on as CEO. Announced on the acquirer's own site: https://banyansoftware.com/2024/06/12/subitup. SubItUp's own site makes no mention of it.

paragraphs: SubItUp sells workforce scheduling and time-management software for shift-based teams. The platform builds staff schedules, lets employees swap and pick up shifts without manager intervention, tracks hours with a built-in time clock, and exports hours worked straight to payroll. A built-in time clock can turn any internet-enabled device into a clock-in point, and hours reconcile automatically before they reach payroll.

The pages name higher education, municipal parks and recreation, healthcare, retail and franchise, and live events among the settings the software is built for. Staff can add, drop, and swap their own shifts with peers, and a manager approves the swap once staff agree to it. Managers set the maximum hours staff can work by role and location, including across teams within one organization.
Payroll exports are built for platforms including ADP, Intuit QuickBooks, Oracle PeopleSoft, Workday, and Paychex. Pricing is based on the number of employees scheduled, with a 10-employee minimum.

before.name: Accela

before.source: ICMA 2025; NRPA 2026; ICMA 2026; NLC City Summit 2026

paragraphs: Accela sells software that government agencies use to run permitting, licensing, and asset management from a single system. Its applications are built for individual government service workflows and can operate together or be deployed only where an agency needs them.

For building departments, intake, plan review, inspections, and permit issuance sit in one workflow rather than in separate disconnected steps. Reviewers from different departments work the same record at once, with annotations and approvals tracked as they happen. Planning teams get the same shared review model, plus automated public notice generation, hearing schedules, and agency notifications. Applicants can see where a case stands and receive consolidated feedback from every reviewing department.

The company says it has thirty years of government expertise built into the product. Testimonials on the site are attributed to municipal staff, including a chief building official in McAllen, Texas. Residents and businesses who encounter Accela through a local agency are directed to that agency rather than to the company.

before.name: CampDoc
before.description: Camp management software with electronic health records for camps, schools, and youth programs

paragraphs: CampDoc sells camp and youth program software built for registration, health management, and day-to-day operations. The buyers are organizations that run programs for children and students, and the company says it powers more than 1,250 camps, youth programs and school programs. Signups, payments, rosters and family-facing workflows sit in one place.

On the health side, staff collect health forms, manage medications, document incidents, and keep records accessible when they need them. The health forms are digital and use conditional logic. Medication administration runs through an eMAR. Attendance, communication, reporting and daily program operations are kept together in one place. Rosters and health records stay aligned across the system.

For IT and compliance reviewers, the company points to SOC 2 Type II controls, role-based access to PHI, single sign-on for organizations that require it, and multi-factor authentication. It also states that the platform is HIPAA and FERPA compliant. Plans start at $355 per month. Onboarding, training, support and compliance are included in every plan, according to the pricing section. Published customer stories include a municipal parks and recreation department that replaced paper forms and manual tracking.

before.name: Bchex
before.description: Background screening and volunteer management for schools and youth-serving organizations

paragraphs: Bchex runs background screening for organizations that have to vet the people they hire, and it also sells continuous monitoring along with visitor and volunteer management. The company advertises that 92% of background checks are delivered in under 24 hours.

A customer requests checks in seconds, tracks progress in real time from a single dashboard, and gets a report at the end. Candidates can scan a driver's license so their information populates automatically instead of being typed in. The platform connects to an applicant tracking system to sync and automate the screening process. Bchex puts terms behind the service: no payment if it misses its turnaround time or if the customer is unsatisfied, and a price match against a cheaper quote.

The company counts more than 2,000 school districts, non-profits, and US businesses among its customers. It states that it processes over 500,000 background checks per year. It describes nearly 30 years spent on this one line of work. The site states that Bchex is SOC 2 Type 2 certified for security, confidentiality, and availability. Buyers pay per order, with no long-term contracts or subscription fees.

before.description: Fleet, fuel, and enterprise asset management software for governments and universities (Volaris) - exhibited at NAFA I&E 2026

paragraphs: AssetWorks builds software, hardware and consulting services for organizations whose work centers on assets and infrastructure. The buyers run commercial fleets or public infrastructure and want to control operating costs.

The fleet system, FleetFocus, is a central platform for maintenance, asset lifecycle tracking, fueling and reporting. A companion product, FuelFocus, watches fuel levels and transactions in real time so discrepancies surface immediately. A mobile extension puts inventory and work order management in the hands of technicians and storekeepers. A Power BI connection supports custom dashboards, advanced reporting and lifecycle analytics on the same data.

The company puts its own history at more than 40 years and the home page counts over 1,000 organizations using the products. Listed offices include one in Berwyn, Pennsylvania and a San Antonio location for education facilities, real estate and planning software. Case studies describe a county internal services department managing roughly 20,000 vehicles. Another covers a regional public transit agency running a fleet of more than 427 active vehicles.

before.name: Eventeny
before.description: Event management SaaS: vendor applications, ticketing, maps, and sponsors for festivals and city events

paragraphs: Eventeny sells event management software that makes it easier to manage vendors, volunteers, attendees, sponsors and maps in one place. The platform is used for festivals, conferences, expos, markets, parades and community gatherings.

Organizers build maps from scratch or on Google Maps with a drag-and-drop event mapping tool. Booths are assigned and spaces connected to tickets from that same place. Vendor and artist applications move through flexible workflows with built-in jury tools. Ticketing covers sales, upgrades and guest check-in with QR codes. Volunteer shifts can be scheduled, team leads assigned, and the crew contacted in one place. Sponsor packages can be customized to fit an event's needs.

Eventeny was started by two founders, Aly Hussaini and Nausheen Punjani. The company says its product marketplace hosts over 4,000 small business owners around the country. Its homepage says more than 2,550,000 users in five or more countries are on Eventeny. It reports over 34,000 events hosted on the platform. Case studies include the City of Suwanee, whose small event team was hosting more than 40 events a year with a primarily paper-based system.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

before.name: Perry Weather
before.description: Weather safety platform: WBGT heat monitoring, lightning alerts, stations and sirens for parks and athletics

paragraphs: Perry Weather sells a weather safety platform that pairs monitoring hardware at a customer site with automated alerting, so an entire staff works from the same reading of conditions. The buyers it names are schools, cities, golf clubs, and industrial firms.

Stations at the customer location measure heat stress, lightning, precipitation, wind, and air quality, refreshing every five minutes in the mobile app and dashboard. Each organization writes its own thresholds and decides who gets notified when one is crossed. Alerts can go to phones or to an outdoor siren system. Countdown timers mark the moment it is safe to resume play or work. All-clears go out automatically once the threat has passed.

Colin Perry founded the company in 2013. It reports more than 5,000 organizations nationwide as customers. It also counts over 200 million alerts sent, covering hazards from heat stress to lightning. Arthur Ventures led a $15M Series B. The stated markets run across athletics, golf, parks and recreation, energy, and airports.

paragraphs: Software Solutions, Inc. sells cloud-based ERP software for public accounting, HR, payroll, and utility billing. The VIP Suite begins with VIP Accounting, which the company calls the core of the Visual Intelligence Portfolio. Other modules listed include budgeting, accounts payable automation, payroll and human resources, employee self-service, and utility billing.

The company has served local governments and utilities since 1978. It became 100% employee-owned in 2004 through an Employee Stock Ownership Plan. The VIP platform launched in 2009. VIP Cloud, a hosted version, was introduced in 2020.

The solutions page says the software is built for the public sector and used by counties, cities, special districts, libraries, and utilities. Utility billing is offered to water districts, electric utilities, and public and private utility companies. The accounting page names the city of Euclid, which it says was outgrowing a spreadsheet bank reconciliation process.

paragraphs: Ankored automates safety and compliance work for youth sports programs, from background checks on adults through to verification of the players themselves. The company says it brings youth and adult requirements under federal, state and governing body standards into one system.

For clubs and leagues that means automated background checks, training and verification for every coach and volunteer. On the player side it handles age and identity verification. It connects to the sport management tools an organization already runs so coach and player records sit together. Automated reminders and audit ready reports take the place of chasing paperwork.

Parks and recreation departments are one of the named audiences, with staff, volunteer and youth compliance managed across programs, sites and seasons. One case study on the site describes a parks department replacing paper forms with a digital system covering 26 recreation centers. The company's writing points to more than thirty states that now require background checks.

before.name: CommunityPass
before.description: Online registration, membership, and payments for parks & rec departments and community schools

paragraphs: CommunityPass is cloud-based software that powers schools, recreation centers, community organizations, and sports leagues. It comes from Capturepoint, whose founder the company names as Joe Oriente.

The product began in 2002 with a town Sports Council overwhelmed by hundreds of paper registration forms as athletic sign-ups climbed. The answer was a single account on one website through which families reach registration for every participating organization in town. Departments can offer registration for classes, activities, programs, and trips, with options to buy merchandise and tickets. Payments accept multiple forms with recurring billing and plans while maintaining PCI compliance.

Check-in and check-out are contactless and digital, with pick-up timestamps and real-time emergency contact information for authorized parents. Staff can choose from 300+ pre-built reports covering attendance, financial, roster, and statistical data, or build their own. The company says CommunityPass has grown to serve parks and recreation organizations and schools all across the country.

paragraphs: Eproval sells permitting software to local government offices that handle special events and film shoots. The platform has since stretched to other complex application and approval work, including government grants and filming approvals.

Each application keeps comments, emails, activity, documents and approvals in one place. Review is coordinated across the departments that have to sign off on a permit. Pricing is one annual subscription with unlimited user licenses. Reports can be built from any data the agency collects. An extra module covers payment and invoicing.

An operations manager quoted on the case studies page says Denver's Office of Special Events gained operational efficiencies after adopting the software. The company says its team has spent more than 20 years building web applications for clients in local government, tourism and chambers of commerce. It describes itself as a SaaS company working in the eGov market. A published corporate social responsibility policy states a commitment to protecting the privacy and security of client data.

paragraphs: HopSkipDrive arranges rides for students who cannot be served by a traditional school bus route. The company calls itself a technology company that solves complex transportation challenges where there is a heightened need for safety, equity, and care.

Rides come through a marketplace connecting kids, older adults, or anyone needing extra support to highly vetted caregivers on wheels. The homepage says rides are licensed, regulated, and ready in six hours. Ride types span McKinney-Vento, foster care, special needs and IEPs, charter schools, general education, after school, and career and technical education. Districts also use RouteWise AI, which optimizes routes for buses and small vehicles.

Denver Public Schools is described on the site as using RouteWise AI to optimize its multimodal transportation system. Cypress-Fairbanks Independent School District decided to outsource its McKinney-Vento and a portion of foster transportation to the company. Counties, government agencies, and nonprofits are also named as groups the company supports. It traces its start to three working moms trying to get their busy kids to and from school and activities.

before.name: Facilitron
before.description: Facility use scheduling, rental and payments platform for school districts

paragraphs: Facilitron connects people looking for event space with the public buildings and fields that can host them. The other half is management software designed for schools, colleges and cities that own those spaces.

Its scheduling platform holds internal bookings and community requests on one calendar, so staff can manage sports practices, plays and other events in the same place. Renters find, request, insure and pay for spaces online. Requests arrive already carrying the organization's own rates, policies and approval workflows. Facilitron collects the payments, automates invoices, facilitates renter insurance and manages credits and refunds. A building automation tie-in schedules HVAC, lighting, irrigation and locks around each event. A separate mobile tool handles California's Williams Act facility inspections.

Facilities from over 15,000 K-12 schools, colleges and municipalities are listed on the marketplace. School districts, municipalities, nonprofits and businesses all use it, whether to lease space out or to find it. The company states that its services are sustained through service fees on external rental amounts rather than direct charges.

before.name: 3rd Eye
before.description: Camera and telematics systems for refuse fleets used by municipal sanitation departments

paragraphs: 3rd Eye sells modular, subscription-based software that runs on top of its own heavy-duty truck camera systems. Its buyers are waste hauling companies that have to manage collection fleets safely and stay connected to their customers. A truck can carry up to eight cameras for a full view around the vehicle.

Video and telematics data upload to the cloud, where they become safety events that a review team turns into driver coaching material. A maintenance module watches the chassis, body and equipment continuously. It hands mechanics a list of repairs ranked by severity or by how long remains before failure. Other modules take on tax paperwork, recording the data behind IFTA reporting and excise fuel tax recovery.

Contamination detection spots recycling contamination and other non-conforming refuse at the point of collection. Adding the route review module helps haulers plan and report the annual reviews that California State Bill 1383 requires. Container quality reviews photograph and geolocate each collection event to find carts needing repair or replacement. The company presents itself as part of Environmental Solutions Group alongside Soft-Pak and Heil, under the Connected Collections banner. Equipment can be taken monthly rather than bought outright, on what the company calls a Hardware as a Service model.

before.name: AMP
before.description: AI robotic sorting systems for recycling facilities (MRFs) - exhibited at SWANA WASTECON 2025

paragraphs: AMP designs, builds, and operates facilities that sort single-stream recycling and municipal solid waste using artificial intelligence. The buyers are waste companies and municipalities, offered sortation services and automation at scale.

The facility product, AMP ONE, is a fully automated sorting plant. It takes in single stream material, municipal solid waste, plant residue and mixed plastics and turns them into bales. Dozens of jet sorters and cameras characterize the stream continuously as it passes. Each finished bale is tagged with a bar code linked to the composition and purity of the material inside it.

For municipal solid waste, AMP states that it operates the facility itself and charges a per-ton processing rate with guaranteed diversion. The company puts typical diversion above 60 percent. It says custom plants can be operational in less than a year. Recovery of target materials is put at more than 90 percent.

paragraphs: CentralSquare Technologies sells software to public agencies, from dispatch centers to city halls. On the public safety side, its suite runs from computer aided dispatch and NG911 call handling through to jail management and analytics. On the administration side, the company says public administrators in over 8,000 communities use it for finance, HR, payroll, asset management, permitting and tax collection.

Public Safety Suite Enterprise connects 911, CAD, RMS, Mobile and Jail in a single platform. A version called Public Safety Suite Pro is designed for small and mid-sized agencies that want one vendor rather than several systems. Vertex NG911 Call Handling gives 911 centers a single platform for voice, text, video and caller location. Vertex also carries built-in text translation and transcription for more than 150 languages, which the company says runs in under 10 seconds. The company says it secures cloud data against cyberattacks through a partnership with Amazon Web Services.

The homepage counts more than 8,000 agencies nationwide as customers. Customers named on the site include the California Highway Patrol. Case studies include the Edgar County 911 team, whose partnership with CentralSquare serves a community of 16,000 residents. Morgan County 911 in Alabama is featured for upgrading to Vertex NG911 Call Handling.

paragraphs: RapidSOS connects public safety agencies, enterprises and large numbers of consumer and corporate devices so emergency information reaches responders. The company states it partners with over 250 enterprise companies and 23,500 public safety agencies.

The premise is that connected systems can share information with responders even before a 911 call is placed. One police department describes adopting a module built around AI-powered live text translation, transcription and call summarization. In an Atlanta deployment, translation covered over 37 languages by voice and over 200 by text. Another center is described using Harmony AI to handle non-emergency calls.

The homepage says agencies and enterprises on the network safeguard over 99% of the country. Published case studies sort customers into categories such as connected vehicles and telematics. One partner statement on the site is attributed to a VP of Safety at Norfolk Southern. A documented problem it addresses is waiting up to ten minutes for a translator on a 911 call.

paragraphs: Vector Solutions sells online training courses and the software to assign, track and report them, to schools and campuses, industrial employers, and fire, EMS and law enforcement agencies. For the fire service that means a training management system that tracks all training, EMS recerts, skill evaluations and ISO requirements in one place. Crews can accept callbacks and shifts from a mobile device, and a companion app handles truck checks, PPE inspections, controlled substance tracking and equipment maintenance. Law enforcement agencies get a training management system built around FTO/PTO and in-service training, plus POST and regulatory management, officer shift scheduling, policy management, BWC audits and accreditation management. A Professional Standards and Early Intervention tool gives agency leaders a way to manage performance and step in early.

In education, the company sells educator and staff training, a student safety and wellness program, and software to manage evaluations and professional development. Colleges get faculty and staff training, campus climate surveys built for VAWA compliance, and incident and EHS management. Industrial employers get a learning management system and course libraries in food safety, industrial skills, paper manufacturing, energy and HR compliance. Federal and military training management, fire marshal and POST training and compliance, and fire and law enforcement academy automation complete the list.

paragraphs: Pace Scheduler sells a cloud-based scheduling system built for organizations that keep 24/7 schedules. Its clients include police departments, sheriff's offices, campus security, fire departments and public transportation agencies. Because that client base varies, the system is modular, so a department's site can be built with only the parts it wants.

The company says it designed the software to be easy to use without dropping the advanced features needed to maintain round-the-clock schedules. A mobile app is included, so staff can view schedules and submit or handle requests from an iOS or Android device as well as from a PC or tablet. In testimonials on the site, departments describe using it to fill shifts, request time off and balance leave banks. One says the shift bidding feature cut a process that used to take a month and a half down to four days.

Those testimonials come from agencies such as Tipp City PD in Ohio, Hudson PD in Colorado, Santa Paula PD in California and the Monroe County Sheriff's Office in Michigan, which says deputies, corrections officers and support staff all use it. Several describe replacing paper or Excel spreadsheets, and one lieutenant says the program replaced over a dozen spreadsheets. The company offers a free online demo to organizations that ask.

paragraphs: Motorola Solutions builds and connects technologies to protect people, property and places, supporting the collaboration between public safety agencies and enterprises. Its public safety lineup includes APX portable and mobile radios and ASTRO radio systems. On the command center side it sells NG911 call routing and call handling and Computer-Aided Dispatch. The company also designs video security and access control systems.

For police users the APX NEXT smart radio comes in single-band and multi-band configurations. The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio adds interoperability, Wi-Fi connectivity and Bluetooth in the vehicle. Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can reach real-time intelligence on the road. Its broadband products can run on FirstNET or on commercial carrier LTE networks. Managed, support and professional services are sold alongside to keep those systems secure and current.

Customer stories on the site include the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Office, Peel Police, Nampa PD and York Regional Police, which serves 1.2 million residents. Hutto Independent School District uses the VB400 body camera to capture evidence in its schools. The home page announces the completed acquisition of D-Fend Solutions, which the company describes as a counter-drone technology firm.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "AI-Powered Solutions Helping ALL First Responders Do Their Best Work" Fetched https://www.govworx.ai. The site is branded GovWorx and the quoted headline ties it directly to the 'software for first responder agencies' description. The buyer is named precisely — 911 Emergency Communications Centers: 'We deliver AI-powered solutions that help ECCs automate tasks and strengthen, guide, and support first responders.' Named products corroborate the sector rather than a same-name firm elsewhere: the CommsCoach suite (QA and call evaluations, pre-hire testing, training and simulations, real-time call guidance) plus MedAssist for paramedics and BluAssist for law enforcement, with claimed scale of 1.2M+ evaluations monthly across 475+ customers. Own primary domain. No concerns.

paragraphs: GovWorx sells CommsCoach, an AI-powered software platform that emergency communications centers use to hire, train, evaluate and support 9-1-1 telecommunicators. It is aimed at the ECC leaders responsible for improving the performance of 9-1-1 professionals. Its modules follow a telecommunicator from candidate through career, linking HIRE, TRAIN, QA and ASSIST in one system, with PROMOTE added for choosing supervisors.

CommsCoach HIRE measures aptitude, resilience, accuracy and composure through structured testing and AI-supported scoring, with tests run onsite or remotely. QA automatically pulls every eligible call and radio transmission, matches transcripts to CAD event data and scores them against the agency's own policies. During live calls, ASSIST listens, transcribes and prompts the call-taker with the policy-specific questions the situation requires. PROMOTE is an evidence-based assessment that identifies leadership potential in supervisor candidates and pairs each result with a personalized development pathway.

An emergency communications administrator at the O'Fallon Police Department in Missouri is quoted saying call-taking compliance rose from single digits to 96% with ASSIST, APCO guidecards and complete QA. In June 2026 APCO International and GovWorx announced a partnership to bring APCO's communications protocols into CommsCoach ASSIST. In August 2026 GovWorx added NEAL, an adaptive non-emergency call handling tool that escalates to a human telecommunicator whenever judgment is needed.

before.name: Aurelian
before.description: AI voice agents answering non-emergency calls for 911 centers - exhibited at APCO 2026

paragraphs: Aurelian builds software for the 911 centers known as public safety answering points. One of its two products answers non-emergency calls instantly, so callers are not left on hold. The other sits with call-takers during emergencies and gives real-time, context-aware guidance without taking control.

The automated line resolves routine calls on its own. It detects and escalates emergencies to a person. During live calls, the guidance tool surfaces the relevant SOP checklist for the incident. It also flags missing information before the call ends. The company says the system learns a center's workflows, SOPs, and systems in order to support the full call flow. Aurelian states that humans remain in control of emergencies and decision-making.

The customers page says PSAPs around the country use Aurelian to cut non-emergency workload and return time to their teams. Published stories include Hamilton County 911 automating more than 300 non-emergency calls a day. The about page says the founders, Max and James, were building call automation technology for hair salons before starting the company. That insight led them to pivot to public safety and build for PSAPs.

quote.text: Automate the calls that don't need a telecommunicator.

provenance.quote: Aurelian is built to support PSAPs before, during, and after every call

before.name: Dimonoff
before.description: Streetlight control nodes and SCMS smart-city management platform for municipalities and utilities

paragraphs: Dimonoff sells smart street lighting control, connecting street and commercial lighting to a single platform so teams can monitor every fixture in real time. The site dates its work in smart street lighting control back to 2006.

A controller fits a NEMA or Zhaga socket on any LED fixture, from any manufacturer, and dims over 0-10V or DALI. The nodes network over Wi-SUN, RF mesh or LTE-M, and keep running their schedule if the link drops. In the office, one interface holds groups, schedules, dimming profiles, faults and reports, and pushes work orders into the asset system a city already runs. The platform also manages nodes from third-party manufacturers, so hardware from a previous supplier does not have to be scrapped. One part number covers supply voltages from 110 to 480 Vac nominal at 50/60 Hz. Node firmware is updated over the air rather than by a crew in a truck.

Networks already running on the platform account for more than 219,500 connected endpoints, by the company's count. Dimonoff states that all of its hardware and software is designed, developed, manufactured and supported in North America. The support FAQ names Groupe Vectanor as the parent company and says it joined the Wi-SUN Alliance as a Contributing Member in April 2026.

before.name: City Detect
before.description: AI cameras on city fleet vehicles detect blight, graffiti, dumping for code enforcement - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026
before.source: ICMA 2025; PWX 2026; ICMA 2026; NLC City Summit 2026

posts_at.label: their own careers page
posts_at.note: moved off Gusto; citydetect.com/careers embeds Gem

paragraphs: City Detect sells a camera and software service that helps municipalities and counties find and address urban blight before complaints pile up. Cameras ride on a city's existing fleet vehicles and collect images of properties as those vehicles drive their normal routes. The company's PASS AI then detects and maps signs of urban blight and decay from the public right of way.

Roof-mounted data collection units capture street-level imagery during routine city operations. Once the images are processed, each detection is assigned a severity score from 1 to 4 and placed on an interactive map. The conditions it picks up run to illegal dumping, tire accumulations, snipe signs, and graffiti. Staff can export timestamped, image-backed reports in a few clicks.

The company says it was founded in 2021. One published case study describes Cathedral City partnering with City Detect in June 2025. For each municipality the company performs local calibration meant to cut false-positive detections and match local rules.

before.name: Archistar
before.description: AI planning and building code assessment tools sold to councils and cities - exhibited at ICMA 2026

paragraphs: Archistar sells AI plan review software to local governments, with a product called AI PreCheck that speeds building code and zoning compliance checks so permits can be issued faster. The same platform is offered to developers, architects and certifiers, who can check compliance before submitting to a municipality or council.

Submitters drag and drop design files onto the platform, which accepts PDF, CAD or BIM formats and reviews them in 2D or 3D. The software then evaluates each submission against the city's local codes and regulations. It is built on generative AI, computer vision and machine learning. Applicants receive standardized reports. For municipalities and councils with particular zoning, planning and compliance requirements, tailored and white-labeled versions are offered.

The company says Archistar was founded by Dr. Benjamin Coorey in 2010 and began life as an education portal. It grew from a university research project into a platform that could read planning rules, run feasibility tests and generate compliant designs in minutes. The site states that Archistar powers digital planning for over 30 cities and governments across Australia, Canada and the United States. Among the municipalities it names supporting are LA County, the City of Los Angeles, the City of Austin and the City of New York. Offices are listed across Los Angeles, Vancouver and Sydney.

paragraphs: Axon sells public safety agencies a connected set of hardware and software: Axon Body 4 cameras, Axon Fleet 3 cameras, TASER 10 energy weapons and drones, unified on a real-time crime center platform with an open ecosystem of integrated partners. The company describes itself as an operating system for public safety. TASER 10, its current less-lethal weapon, can deploy up to 10 individually targeted probes without reloading when de-escalation fails.

Axon Fusus puts officer location, alerts, dispatch data, ALPR overlays and video feeds on a single live map so command, field and real-time crime center teams work from the same picture. Residents and businesses can opt in through Community Connect to share their camera video, and those cameras then appear on the Fusus map. The Axon AI Era Plan bundles current and future Axon AI products for a fixed annual cost. Among them is Draft One, which generates first-draft report narratives from audio transcripts of digital evidence and details the officer narrates. Axon Assistant, a voice assistant on the Body 4 camera, translates conversations when no human interpreter is available.

Chief Gary Berg of Campbell PD is quoted saying Fusus lets him see live location, alerts and video from body cams, drones and public safety cameras in one platform. Axon says it is on a mission to cut gun-related deaths between police and the public in half by 2033 through technology, training and trust.

We are on a mission to cut gun-related deaths between police and public in half by 2033 through technology, training and trust.

before.name: PowerSchool
before.description: Student information system giant plus enrollment, comms, and analytics - exhibited at CoSN 2026

paragraphs: PowerSchool sells software that school districts run from home to classroom to central office, covering the records, communication, and back-office work of running a school system. The company says its software reaches over 60 million students in 90 countries.

The student information side pulls scattered records into one accurate student record, so staff and families are working from the same source. Teaching and learning products sit alongside it, among them a learning management system. For the central office, finance, human resources, and operations are brought into one connected system. A separate data practice centralizes information that would otherwise sit in district silos.

PowerBuddy, the company's AI assistant, is described as built for students, families, teachers, and administrators. It is also pitched at IT staff and data analysts working with district data. PowerSchool states that PowerBuddy won a 2024 GESS Education Award. In districts already using its products, the company says teachers are reclaiming at least 10 hours a week.

A second line goes into pork and poultry barns, where the company says its products help assure livestock health. A third covers refrigeration, with controls that supermarkets, convenience stores and liquor stores use to hold groceries at temperature.

A water chemistry controller watches the pool continuously and decides when the water needs attention. Operators reach those controllers through an online service the company describes as simple and secure. On the livestock side, the systems track feed inventory across a farm and send real-time data back to feed mills.

The company was incorporated in 1991. Its original ownership group has remained unchanged and has been together for over 30 years. More than 50,000 controllers have been designed and manufactured over that period. All manufacturing is performed onsite at a facility in Saint Louis, Missouri. The BECSys line of water treatment controllers was introduced in 2005. Before that, many products were marketed and distributed under the names of partner organizations.

before.name: Greenzie
before.description: Autonomous mowing software retrofitting commercial mowers, sold via OEMs to grounds and parks crews

paragraphs: Greenzie makes self-driving software meant to improve the safety, productivity and profitability of a landscaping fleet. It partners with OEMs to manufacture Greenzie-equipped, Robotic Ready mowers sold at outdoor power equipment dealers throughout the United States. Buyers shop for those mowers at dealer locations nationwide.

Each Greenzie-equipped mower carries sensors the company says are field tested for obstacle avoidance, smooth driving and clean stripes. Operators can switch between manual and autonomous modes. A crew mows the perimeter once and lets the software finish the job while they move on to other tasks. The software is designed in accordance with ANSI/RIA R15.08-1-2020 safety requirements for industrial robots.

The customers are commercial landscaping crews, and the company frames its work as making jobs easier, faster and safer for large landscapers across the country. Greenzie began in 2018, when co-founder Charles Brian Quinn started calling every landscaper he could reach. The team describes itself as roboticists, software engineers and landscaping professionals. It says it is backed by venture capital firms and investors.

before.name: Colorado Time Systems
before.description: Aquatic timing systems, touchpads, scoreboards, and meet management software for municipal pools (PlayCore)

paragraphs: Colorado Time Systems makes timing and scoring equipment for aquatic sports, with a broad offering of timing systems for those events. The buyers are aquatic and sporting facilities. The company also publishes planning resources for architects, designers, aquatic consultants and facility owners.

Touchpads are described as lightweight, dependable and internally sealed, detecting even the lightest touch. Start systems include an entry-level model for swimming. Deck plates carry the plug-in connections for touchpads and backup pushbuttons. Scoreboards come as permanent, portable or wireless options, including shot clocks and horns. Multisport scoreboards sit in a powder-coated 5052-alloy aluminum chassis. The diving line is stated to comply with NFHS, NCAA, USA Diving and FINA rules.

The company says it has designed and delivered equipment for over 50 years. It states that it is the Official Scoring and Timing System of USA Water Polo. It also names itself the Official Scoring Partner of USA Diving.

before.name: Forerunner
before.description: Floodplain management software: NFIP/CRS compliance, elevation certificates; $26.3M Series B - exhibited at StormCon 2026

paragraphs: Forerunner sells software it calls a geospatial intelligence layer. The platform unifies geospatial data, field operations, and AI-powered workflows in one place. Local government is a core buyer, with compliance work across stormwater, floodplain, and code enforcement programs. The company also markets to energy and infrastructure operators handling inspections across active sites and assets.

At the base sits a map-first view holding every asset, permit parcel, violation, and environmental layer. On top of it run configurable workflows for inspections, permits, violations, and grant tracking. Inspection findings then generate corrective actions, and permit deadlines trigger notifications. The company says adoption brings no rip-and-replace projects and no major workflow disruptions. It claims teams are up and running in weeks.

Published case studies name the Puerto Rico Planning Board, which the company says replaced paper forms and spreadsheets for field inspections and code compliance. Another states that Lee County saves approximately 16 hours of staff time per week. A further case study describes Ponce Inlet centralizing National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System workflows to reclaim 10 or more hours per week.

before.name: GovWell
before.description: AI permitting and licensing platform: 24/7 resident assistant, AI code-compliance review - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026, Maryland Municipal League 2026
before.source: ICMA 2025; NACo 2026; ICMA 2026; NLC City Summit 2026; Maryland Municipal League 2026

paragraphs: GovWell sells software that city and county governments use to run permitting, licensing, planning, and code enforcement work. Residents and businesses use the same system to reach services, pay, and get answers outside office hours.

Permits, plan review, and inspections are handled together in one place for staff. Licensing runs online too, with applicants filing, paying, and renewing while staff keep records and approvals on their side. Code enforcement officers track cases, schedule inspections, and follow issues to closure. The company argues that AI can do real work in these processes, reviewing applications against local code, answering resident questions, flagging violations in plans, and routing inspections.

GovWell says it was founded by the son of a general contractor who watched his father struggle to get permits quickly. Its case for existing is that local governments cannot hire software engineers at competitive salaries. Deployment strategists and configuration tooling are meant to shorten implementations against older systems.

paragraphs: Archistar sells AI plan review software to local governments, with a product called AI PreCheck that speeds building code and zoning compliance checks so permits can be issued faster. The same platform is offered to developers, architects and certifiers, who can check compliance before submitting to a municipality or council.

Submitters drag and drop design files onto the platform, which accepts PDF, CAD or BIM formats and reviews them in 2D or 3D. The software then evaluates each submission against the city's local codes and regulations. It is built on generative AI, computer vision and machine learning. Applicants receive standardized reports. For municipalities and councils with particular zoning, planning and compliance requirements, tailored and white-labeled versions are offered.

The company says Archistar was founded by Dr. Benjamin Coorey in 2010 and began life as an education portal. It grew from a university research project into a platform that could read planning rules, run feasibility tests and generate compliant designs in minutes. The site states that Archistar powers digital planning for over 30 cities and governments across Australia, Canada and the United States. Among the municipalities it names supporting are LA County, the City of Los Angeles, the City of Austin and the City of New York. Offices are listed across Los Angeles, Vancouver and Sydney.

paragraphs: City Detect sells a camera and software service that helps municipalities and counties find and address urban blight before complaints pile up. Cameras ride on a city's existing fleet vehicles and collect images of properties as those vehicles drive their normal routes. The company's PASS AI then detects and maps signs of urban blight and decay from the public right of way.

Roof-mounted data collection units capture street-level imagery during routine city operations. Once the images are processed, each detection is assigned a severity score from 1 to 4 and placed on an interactive map. The conditions it picks up run to illegal dumping, tire accumulations, snipe signs, and graffiti. Staff can export timestamped, image-backed reports in a few clicks.

The company says it was founded in 2021. One published case study describes Cathedral City partnering with City Detect in June 2025. For each municipality the company performs local calibration meant to cut false-positive detections and match local rules.

paragraphs: e-PlanSoft sells electronic plan review software, and its suite of products is offered to both public and private sectors. e-PlanREVIEW is a web-based electronic plan review solution on which several reviewers can mark up plans at the same time. goPost is a Citizen Self-Service portal where applicants apply for permits, submit plans for review, and download reviewed and approved plans.

brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile_research.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

before.name: Computronix
before.description: POSSE permitting, licensing and regulatory platform for state and local agencies

paragraphs: Computronix sells off-the-shelf software solutions for permitting, licensing, alcoholic beverage control, and gaming control. Those products run on POSSE, a web-based platform for automating permitting, licensing, enforcement and compliance workflows.

The permitting product automates workflows for building, planning, engineering, permitting, inspections and code enforcement. The alcoholic beverage control product manages the business and data behind liquor licensing, compliance and enforcement. The gaming product is aimed at agencies seeking a risk-based regulatory model for the gaming industry. The company says the software is engineered to comply with high security and regulatory compliance standards, including NIST, FedRAMP and ISO. Newer offerings include AI-powered portal assistance that helps applicants find answers and navigate permitting processes.

Computronix was founded in 1979 by Herman Leusink. It describes growing from a single employee to nearly two hundred employees and dozens of clients in major population centers across North America. One case study covers the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission, which regulates and controls that state's alcoholic beverage industry. The same alcohol system is used in nine other states and two provinces for alcohol industry regulation. Another case study describes the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario using POSSE ABC for liquor control, gaming, horse racing and recreational cannabis.

before.name: GeoCivix
before.description: Cloud permitting, plan review, inspections, and code enforcement for local gov and fire districts

paragraphs: GeoCivix sells cloud-based software that cities, counties and municipalities use to run permitting, licensing, inspections, plan review and citizen services from one system. The pitch is a replacement for paper-based workflows with digital applications, automated routing, electronic plan review, mobile inspections and online payments.

Applicants use a government portal open around the clock, where they manage their projects and pay fees without calling or coming into the office. Staff mark up documents and let the system automate routing. Notifications and comment letters go back out to applicants as reviews move along. Inspectors work from a tablet or smart phone in the field, taking photos, creating reports and managing workloads on site. Permits, inspections, plans, documents, notes and approvals stay organized in one place.

Staff, reviewers, inspectors, citizens and contractors all work from the same project record. An implementation team starts by collecting application forms, communication templates, fee formulas and document workflows for configuration. The company says many agencies launch initial workflows in as little as 6 weeks, with full deployment typically completed within a few months. Every subscription is said to include unlimited technical support for all users. Listed integrations include ESRI ArcGIS, Bluebeam Revu, Cityworks, Infor/Hansen, FireRMS, Laserfiche and payment systems.

before.name: Avolve Software
before.description: ProjectDox electronic plan review for building, fire, planning, and public works agencies - exhibited at ICMA 2026

paragraphs: Avolve sells electronic plan review software to state and local government agencies. The product agencies implement for that work is ProjectDox. Customers quoted on the site also name a second product, DigEplan.

The software carries a review from the applicant's submission through to completion. Avolve describes the plan review as having GIS, AI and field mobility embedded. It is meant to fit whatever permitting stack an agency already runs. In a published case study, a water and sewer commission reviews about 3,500 plan submittals and 34,000 permit transactions a year. After implementing ProjectDox, that agency reported review times falling from eight weeks to two or three.

That commission serves more than 1.9 million people. Avolve says its plan review is built on insight from more than 350 government customers. Testimonials on its site come from cities and counties, including one crediting ProjectDox with improving operations across Minneapolis.

quote.text: Gone are the days when one has to pick up a telephone and call to ask, ‘Where is my plan in the process?’

paragraphs: Clariti sells community development software to local governments, pitched at any size and budget. One edition is permitting software for large local governments. paragraphs: Cloudpermit sells online public works and community development software meant to help local governments modernize. The promise is a system that is easier for staff and better for residents.

Building permit applications come in online and permits can be issued as soon as payment is processed. Land use review covers rezonings, variances, subdivisions, site plans and public hearings. before.source: ICMA 2025; NACo 2026; ICMA 2026; NLC City Summit 2026

paragraphs: Deckard Technologies sells software that local governments use to deal with residential property problems in their jurisdictions. The products cover short-term rentals, long-term rentals, and foreclosed and vacant properties.

The short-term rental product monitors a jurisdiction by analyzing more than 15 million listings from over 10,000 rental websites in real time. The vacancy and foreclosure side watches court records and mortgage reassignments instead. Other tools handle transient occupancy tax filings and payments. A published case study describes a city adopting the Rentalscape platform in 2024 with a structured letter outreach campaign, in which the vendor develops the mailing list and generates, prints and mails the letters to identified hosts.

The company was founded in May 2018 by Greg Rose, Jess Flanagan and Tony Moriarty, starting in both Australia and the United States. It now keeps offices in the United States, Colombia and Australia. Its own count of customers is more than 500 jurisdictions worldwide. The company timeline records several seed rounds, among them a Seed-4 raise.

quote.text: aims to empower local governments with the data, insights, and tools they need to maximize compliance and unlock vital public revenue.
